transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-05-27 15:00 UTC
Duration: 39 minutes
Attendees: Liam (Redwood AE), Sofia (Redwood SE), Marcus (CTO Bluebridge), Priya (Lead ML Engineer), Julian (Product)

Summary: quick hosted API demo focused on chat and text-gen basics — streaming behavior, key generation parameters (max_tokens, temperature, top_p, stop), retry and idempotency patterns, and how the console exposes latency/cost. Customer is evaluating hosted onramp for a pilot (customer-facing chat assistant) but is sensitive to latency and P95 tail; they also mentioned regulatory data retention constraints and want to understand encryption/KMS.

Topics covered: Hosted chat endpoints, streaming vs non-streaming, token accounting and cost signals in console, parameterization strategies for quality vs latency, retry/backoff and idempotency tokens, prefix caching and KV cache brief, demo of console request/response metrics, next steps: benchmarks and security docs.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Liam: hey everyone good afternoon, thanks for joining from bluebridge. i'm liam from redwood. we'll keep this to about 35 ish minutes, run through hosted chat quickstart and a couple resiliency patterns, and save time for your questions.
[00:10] Marcus: awesome yeah thanks, we only have like 40 minutes so appreciate the tight agenda.
[00:18] Sofia: hi all, i'm sofia on the redwood solutions engineering side, i'll run the console and show some live behavior with streaming and retries.
[00:25] Priya: hi, quick note — for us latency is critical, p95 under 350ms ideally, and we have a mix of short and longer prompts, also interested in data retention / encryption.
[00:36] Liam: got it, we'll show how to tune for that, and talk through hosted vs dedicated briefly if it comes up.
[00:46] Sofia: okay i'm going to pull up the console, if anyone hasn't used redwood console before it's a lightweight dashboard. i'm starting a live request to the hosted chat endpoint — i'm sending a short user prompt like 'summarize the following product note' so we can see streaming tokens.
[01:10] Sofia: (typing) you should see the stream come in — this is chunked server-sent events style, each event shows a delta of tokens, you can render progressively in the client.
[01:24] Julian: nice, so the client gets partial pieces as they arrive, that's good for UX.
[01:29] Sofia: yep — note that streaming mode doesn't change token accounting, cost is per token generated same as non-stream. also you can control latency by adjusting max_tokens and using early stop tokens.
[01:45] Marcus: how do retries work if a stream fails mid-response?
[01:52] Sofia: good question — we recommend an idempotency key per user-turn so retries can be deduped on the gateway. for partial streams, the client should re-request with same idempotency token and our gateway can return the completed cached response if it finished server-side, otherwise we re-run with deterministic seeds if available. sometimes transcriptions call it i d key or idemp.
[02:18] Priya: are you doing any prefix caching or KV cache so repeated system prompts aren't recomputed?
[02:25] Sofia: yes, the platform supports prefix/KV cache — if you have repeated system prompts or long contexts we can cache the KV for the model so subsequent calls skip the attention recompute. small caveat, that's more effective for longer lived sessions and requires model variant that supports kv cache. it shows up in the console as cache hits/misses in the latency breakdown.
[02:47] Marcus: can you show the console cost/latency breakdown?
[02:51] Sofia: sure, switching to the route dashboard — here's token-level cost by model and a latency waterfall: network, gateway, model execution. you can see p50/p95 and also token counts per call. if you set a target e.g., p95 under 350ms, the console helps suggest changes like moving to a smaller model for short prompts or enabling prefix cache.
[03:20] Liam: quick note on models — hosted catalog has vetted open models and some quantized variants. smallest fast variants cost less and are order-of-magnitude faster but may have lower quality on long-form. balancing temperature and top_p also affects token churn — higher temperature can lead to longer responses, which increases cost and latency.
[03:48] Priya: what about retries/backoff strategy you recommend? we saw some transient 5xx from previous vendors.
[03:55] Sofia: we usually recommend immediate 1-2 fast retries with exponential backoff and jitter for gateway-level 5xx; for streaming partial responses use idempotency keys and client-side rehydration. server will return 409 if duplicate in flight. for throttling 429s, implement token bucket on client and exponential backoff with retry-after from headers.
[04:25] Marcus: curious about idempotency semantics — if a retry happens and the original actually completed, do you return the same content?
[04:33] Sofia: yes if the original request completed within our window and the idempotency token is same we return the stored response. there is a short retention window for idempotent responses — default 5 minutes for hosted, configurable for dedicated.
[04:47] Priya: is that retention window documented?
[04:50] Liam: yes, sofia will attach the docs and surface the config options in the deck we send.
[04:57] Sofia: quick demo: i'll purposely throttle the route to trigger a 429 to show the headers and retry-after. (small pause) there you go, see retry-after: 12 seconds, and the console suggests a backoff.
[05:20] Julian: what's the recommended client-side UX for showing the user during backoffs? do you push partial tokens then show a spinner?
[05:27] Sofia: depends on product — many teams show partial stream and then a subtle reconnect indicator; don't drop the partial content. for short responses you might buffer until first chunk to avoid flicker.
[05:40] Marcus: about encryption — we need customer-managed keys (KMS/HSM) for content at rest and in transit, can hosted support that?
[05:48] Liam: hosted supports KMS for logs and stored artifacts; for full HSM-backed key control and on-prem key custody you may look at private deployment. we'll link the security whitepaper.
[06:03] Priya: what about data retention — we can't have training data retention, must be able to opt out.
[06:09] Liam: by default hosted does not use customer input to train models; we also provide retention controls and audit logs. again we'll attach the specific policy docs.
[06:22] Marcus: great. can you walk through parameter tradeoffs — like temp, top_p, and max tokens — and how they relate to cost?
[06:30] Sofia: yeah, so max_tokens sets the upper bound of generative tokens; cost scales linearly with tokens. temperature/top_p control output diversity: higher temp typically increases output length unpredictably, which can increase tokens. top_p shaping can sometimes reduce length by focusing distribution. For latency you can cap max_tokens and use stop sequences to keep responses concise. we also recommend using deterministic sampling (low temp) for transactional answers to improve cache hit rates.
[07:05] Priya: so lowering temperature helps caching because same prompt yields similar responses?
[07:09] Sofia: exactly — deterministic outputs increased cacheability. additionally, seed control can help.
[07:16] Julian: do you expose partial token latency metrics per model?
[07:19] Sofia: per-model latency breakdown yes — you can see token generation rate and prefix overhead. that helps you pick a model variant tuned for short-form or long-form.
[07:34] Marcus: if we wanted to pilot with 100 requests per second spiky to 1k, how would hosted handle that?
[07:42] Liam: hosted auto scales but subject to regional capacity; for predictable high spikes we recommend dedicated reserved capacity or request burst increases. we can map your traffic profile and propose a burst policy.
[07:58] Priya: how does concurrent requests affect KV cache?
[08:02] Sofia: KV cache is per-model-worker; high concurrency can reduce effective cache hit rate if requests spread across many workers. batching and sticky routing help — there's a console knob for affinity if you're on dedicated.
[08:18] Marcus: can you show a sample API request for streaming with idempotency header?
[08:22] Sofia: sure, (reads) POST /v1/chat/stream with header X-Idempotency-Key: <uuid>, Accept: text/event-stream; body contains messages array plus max_tokens and temperature. I'll paste the sample in chat.
[08:39] Priya: are there SDKs that implement streaming client helpers?
[08:43] Liam: yes we have official SDKs in JS/Python that handle SSE and reconnect patterns. sample code repo link will be included.
[08:53] Sofia: i'm toggling response mode to non-stream to show the full response latency vs streaming — note generation latency is same but perceived latency differs because streaming shows partial content earlier.
[09:05] Julian: any tips to reduce token usage for system prompts? ours are long policy texts.
[09:11] Sofia: compress system prompts — store the policy in a reference doc and pass a short pointer plus a condensed instruction. prefix cache helps too; another pattern is deterministic summarization step that runs once and stores the summary.
[09:29] Marcus: about failure modes, do you have graceful degradation patterns? e.g., if model is slow fallback to smaller model?
[09:36] Sofia: yes — smart routing policy can fallback to a cheap variant or pre-synthesized canned responses. we can set canary or A/B rollouts and automatic fallback chain in route config. console has a route policy editor.
[09:54] Priya: do you expose per-route SLOs?
[09:57] Liam: yes, you can set target SLOs and get alerts. Hosted offers best-effort targets; for SLA-backed commitments you'd look at dedicated with contract.
[10:08] Marcus: competition question — how do you compare on p95 and cost to openai?
[10:14] Liam: we publish benchmarks for common models; typically for open model variants we see competitive cost and with our batching/cache optimizations we get better cost/throughput for sustained workloads. we'll send a tailored comparison.
[10:25] Sofia: i'm going to run a short synthetic load (demo) to show p95 behavior — note this is a small sandbox not your production traffic. starting now.
[10:40] Sofia: load finished — you can see p50 ~160ms, p95 ~340ms on the route with caching on. turning caching off the p95 jumps and token time increases.
[10:55] Marcus: that p95 is close to our target. what about tail spikes during GC or probes?
[11:03] Sofia: we instrument tail events — console has traces and an error distribution view so you can attach spans to tokens. if you want strict tails we normally recommend dedicated with pinned workers.
[11:19] Priya: let's talk about observability — can we attach request-level traces to our APM?
[11:24] Liam: yes we provide tracing hooks and can emit logs to your SIEM or cloud log sink; we also have distributed tracing correlation ids.
[11:34] Julian: any gotchas for streaming over flaky mobile networks?
[11:38] Sofia: mobile networks benefit from chunk-wise buffering and resume strategies; keep idempotency keys and rehydrate on reconnect. limit max chunk size to avoid long delays.
[11:51] Marcus: question on rate limiting per-user vs per-api-key?
[11:55] Liam: both — you can set quotas at key, route, or user level; for per-user enforcement you pass a user identifier.
[12:05] Priya: last tech question — how do you measure tokenization differences? we've seen token counts vary across tokenizers.
[12:11] Sofia: we publish tokenizer tools and per-model tokenization rules; console token counts use the model's tokenizer. if you have custom pre-tokenization we'll help map metrics.
[12:27] Liam: ok time check — about 10 minutes left. we'll skip some deep config but summarize and capture action items.
[12:34] Marcus: sounds good, important next step for us is a short pilot with 2 endpoints and sample traffic pattern.
[12:40] Liam: we'll propose a pilot plan and pricing, sofia will include benchmark plan.
[12:45] Priya: also we need the SOC2 and KMS docs before legal review.
[12:50] Liam: yes will attach both.
[12:53] Julian: quick thing — can you show a retry timeline example in the console?
[12:57] Sofia: yup, toggling to request logs — here's a 5xx followed by retry with same idempotency token returning cached response. look, timeline shows first attempt ended at t=0.9s then retry-attempt returned cached payload at t=1.2s.
[13:17] Marcus: ok that's helpful.
[13:20] Liam: any other questions?
[13:23] Priya: not from me.
[13:25] Julian: no.
[13:27] Marcus: no, let's wrap. thanks.

Recap / Key takeaways:
- Hosted supports streaming and non-streaming; streaming improves perceived latency but token cost is same.
- Use idempotency keys (X-Idempotency-Key) to dedupe retries and support partial stream rehydration.
- Prefix/KV cache reduces compute for repeated context; effective for longer sessions or repeated system prompts.
- Console shows token-level cost and latency waterfall; helpful for tuning p95 tradeoffs.
- For strict tail latency or heavy sustained spiky load, consider dedicated reserved capacity.
